lead: Real pipelines rarely run as one straight pipe. A pump feeds branches that split and rejoin, or lengths of different diameter joined end to end. This chapter gives two rules. In series, every pipe carries the same discharge and the head losses add. In parallel, the same head loss drives every branch and the discharges add. With these rules a whole network becomes one equivalent pipe: a single length and diameter that gives the same total discharge for the same total head loss. That is how designers size mains and check whether a branch gets enough flow.
prereq: You need: Darcy-Weisbach friction factor, major and minor losses, and HGL and TEL.

sections.h3: Series pipes: one discharge, losses add

blocks.text: Two pipes in series are joined end to end. The same discharge Q passes through both, because no fluid is stored or lost at the joint. The total head loss is the sum of the losses in each pipe plus any minor loss at the joint: H = Σh<sub>fi</sub> + Σh<sub>mi</sub>. For straight pipes, Darcy-Weisbach gives h<sub>f</sub> = f(L/D)(V²/2g) = 8fLQ²/(π²gD⁵). Here f is the friction factor (dimensionless), L is length (m), D is diameter (m), Q is discharge (m³/s), V is mean velocity (m/s), and g = 9.81 m/s².

For the same f and a chosen equivalent diameter D<sub>e</sub>, the equivalent length L<sub>e</sub> satisfies L<sub>e</sub>/D<sub>e</sub>⁵ = Σ(L<sub>i</sub>/D<sub>i</sub>⁵). Note the fifth power: a short narrow pipe can add more loss than a long wide one. Series equivalent length is not a simple sum of lengths.

sections.h3: Parallel pipes: one head loss, discharges add

blocks.text: Two pipes in parallel leave a node A and rejoin at node B. Both see the same pressure difference, so the head loss from A to B is the same through each branch: h<sub>f1</sub> = h<sub>f2</sub> = H. The total discharge is the sum: Q = Q₁ + Q₂ + ...

For the same f, hf = 8fLQ²/(π²gD⁵) gives Q ∝ √(D⁵/L). Thus Q₁/Q₂ = √[(D₁⁵/L₁)/(D₂⁵/L₂)]. If all parallel pipes have the same D and f, 1/√Le = Σ1/√Li. A longer branch carries less flow, not more. Use HGL and TEL to see that both branches start and end at the same energy levels.

sections.h3: Equivalent pipe: one pipe replacing the network

blocks.text: An equivalent pipe is a single pipe that carries the same total Q for the same total head loss H as the original system. To find it:

items: Replace each series run by one length using L<sub>e</sub>/D<sub>e</sub>⁵ = ΣL<sub>i</sub>/D<sub>i</sub>⁵ at a chosen D<sub>e</sub>.
Replace parallel branches by one length using 1/√L<sub>e</sub> = Σ1/√L<sub>i</sub> when D and f are equal.
If diameters or f differ, write h<sub>f</sub> = 8fLQ²/(π²gD⁵) for each branch, set head losses equal in parallel, add Q in parallel, and solve.

blocks.text: Include minor losses by adding their h<sub>m</sub> = K(V²/2g) to the branch head loss, or by an equivalent length L<sub>e</sub> = KD/f. Check units: L and D in metres, Q in m³/s.

examples.question: Two parallel pipes connect the same two nodes. Pipe 1: L₁ = 100 m, D₁ = 0.10 m. Pipe 2: L₂ = 200 m, D₂ = 0.10 m. Both have f = 0.02. The total flow is Q = 0.03 m³/s. Find the flow in each pipe and the equivalent length at D = 0.10 m. Neglect minor losses.
steps: For parallel pipes, h<sub>f1</sub> = h<sub>f2</sub>. With h<sub>f</sub> = 8fLQ²/(π²gD⁵) and equal f, D, g: L₁Q₁² = L₂Q₂².
Equivalent length for equal D and f: 1/√L<sub>e</sub> = 1/√100 + 1/√200 = 0.1000 + 0.0707 = 0.1707 m<sup>-1/2</sup>. So L<sub>e</sub> = 1/(0.1707)² = 34.3 m.
examples.answer: Q₁ = 0.0176 m³/s, Q₂ = 0.0124 m³/s, and the equivalent length is L<sub>e</sub> = 34.3 m at D = 0.10 m.
examples.check:
import math
Q = 0.03
L1 = 100.0
L2 = 200.0
r = math.sqrt(L2 / L1)
Q2 = Q / (1 + r)
Q1 = r * Q2
Le = 1.0 / ((1 / math.sqrt(L1) + 1 / math.sqrt(L2)) ** 2)
print(round(Q1, 4))
print(round(Q2, 4))
print(round(Le, 1))

traps: In series, adding discharges is wrong: every series pipe has the same Q.
In parallel, adding head losses is wrong: every branch has the same h<sub>f</sub> between the two nodes.
For a series equivalent length use L<sub>e</sub>/D<sub>e</sub>⁵ = ΣL<sub>i</sub>/D<sub>i</sub>⁵, not L<sub>e</sub> = ΣL<sub>i</sub>.
Use D in metres and Q in m³/s in h<sub>f</sub> = 8fLQ²/(π²gD⁵); mixing mm and m gives large errors.
A longer parallel branch carries less flow when D and f are equal, because Q ∝ 1/√L.

quiz.q: State the two rules for pipes in series.
quiz.a: Same discharge Q through each pipe; total head loss is the sum of individual head losses.

quiz.q: State the two rules for parallel pipes.
quiz.a: Same head loss across each branch; total discharge is the sum of branch discharges.

quiz.q: Why is series equivalent length not ΣL<sub>i</sub>?
quiz.a: Head loss varies as L/D⁵, so a small D adds much more loss; equivalent length must weight each L<sub>i</sub> by D<sub>e</sub>⁵/D<sub>i</sub>⁵.

quiz.q: Two equal-length parallel pipes have diameters D and 2D, same f. Find the flow ratio for the same head loss.
A pipe of L = 50 m, D = 0.05 m is replaced by D<sub>e</sub> = 0.10 m at the same f. Find the equivalent length.
In the worked example, which pipe carries more flow and why?
quiz.a: Pipe 1, because equal head loss and same D, f means Q ∝ 1/√L; L₁ < L₂.

quiz.q: A parallel branch is made longer but total Q is fixed. What happens to the flow in the other branch?
quiz.a: The longer branch has higher resistance, so its Q falls. For fixed total Q, the other branch Q rises; the common head loss adjusts.

beyond: Not for the exam. Looped water-distribution networks need simultaneous equations for every node; the Hardy Cross method and modern EPANET software solve them. Engineers use equivalent-pipe ideas to size colony water mains and to check whether the last flat in a block gets adequate pressure. Search for Hardy Cross method, pipe network analysis, and EPANET if you want to go further.
